summary: Christ as judge; the basis of judgment; the destinies of the just and the unjust
readingInstruction: Read Revelation 20:11-15, Matthew 25:31-46, and 2 Corinthians 5:10. Today is a doctrinal pause on the final judgment. It is a serious subject, so read slowly, and notice both the justice and the mercy that appear in these passages.
settingTheScene: Christians have confessed from the earliest days that Christ “will come again to judge the living and the dead.” The final judgment is not a minor topic; Jesus spoke of it often, and the apostles preached it. It is meant to produce reverence, sobriety, and urgency, and for believers, thankfulness and hope. We must handle it with care because it concerns real people and eternal consequences.
observation: “Then I saw a great white throne and him who was seated on it” (Revelation 20:11).
“And I saw the dead, great and small, standing before the throne, and books were opened” (Revelation 20:12).
“The dead were judged by what was written in the books, according to what they had done” (Revelation 20:12).
“And if anyone’s name was not found written in the book of life, he was thrown into the lake of fire” (Revelation 20:15).
“He will separate people one from another as a shepherd separates the sheep from the goats” (Matthew 25:32).
“As you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me” (Matthew 25:40).
“And these will go away into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life” (Matthew 25:46).
“For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each one may receive what is due for what he has done in the body, whether good or evil” (2 Corinthians 5:10).
doctrinalFocus:
The final judgment is the public, universal, and final assessment by Christ of every human being at the end of history. The Bible teaches several truths about it.

It is certain. God “has fixed a day on which he will judge the world in righteousness by a man whom he has appointed” (Acts 17:31). Jesus himself is the judge (John 5:22; 2 Timothy 4:1), which means the one who died for sinners is the one before whom all will stand. It is universal: “the dead, great and small.” No one is overlooked or excused.

It is according to truth and works. The books record what each person has done, and the judgment will be perfectly just. Nothing is hidden (Luke 12:2-3; Romans 2:16). Works are the evidence of the heart. Yet no one is saved by works. The decisive question is whether one’s name is in the book of life, the book of the Lamb who was slain (Revelation 13:8; 21:27). Those who are in Christ are declared righteous by faith, and “there is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1). Believers will also appear before the judgment seat of Christ, but not for condemnation. Paul says the judgment will evaluate their works, to bring rewards or loss, “yet so as through fire” (1 Corinthians 3:12-15). Their salvation is secure, and their service will be rewarded by grace. The judgment of the nations in Matthew 25 shows that how people treat Christ’s people (the “least of these”) shows their relationship to him.

It results in two outcomes. The Bible teaches the final separation of the saved and the lost: eternal life and eternal punishment (Matthew 25:46; Daniel 12:2). The majority of Christian teaching throughout history has understood this punishment as conscious and everlasting, and this view has strong support in Matthew 25:41-46, Mark 9:43-48, 2 Thessalonians 1:9, and Revelation 14:11 and 20:10. A minority of evangelicals, including some respected teachers such as John Stott, have argued for conditional immortality or annihilationism, the view that the lost will be destroyed and cease to exist after judgment, pointing to passages that speak of “destruction” and “perishing.” The universalist view, that all will eventually be saved, has been rejected by the church as contrary to Scripture’s clear teaching. We should handle this topic with humility, not with relish. “As I live, declares the Lord GOD, I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked” (Ezekiel 33:11).

What should we do with this doctrine? It should fill us with a sober urgency to share the gospel (2 Corinthians 5:11), with confidence that God will right every wrong (Romans 12:19), with comfort for those who suffer injustice, and with humility, because we also deserve judgment apart from grace. It should lead us to live in a way that is pleasing to the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:9). And it should drive us to Christ, who bore the judgment for all who trust him, so that on that day we can stand in him.
interpretation:
John sees a great white throne. The white signifies purity, and the throne’s size signifies the greatness of the occasion. “From his presence earth and sky fled away, and no place was found for them.” The old creation cannot stand before the Judge. The dead are raised, “great and small,” and stand before the throne. Books are opened, and “another book was opened, which is the book of life.” The books record deeds, the book of life records the names of those who belong to the Lamb. The sea, Death, and Hades give up their dead. Then “Death and Hades were thrown into the lake of fire. This is the second death, the lake of fire. And if anyone’s name was not found written in the book of life, he was thrown into the lake of fire.”

Matthew 25 gives a parable of the same event. The Son of Man sits on his throne of glory, and all nations are gathered before him. He separates people as a shepherd separates sheep from goats. To the sheep he says, “Come, you who are blessed by my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.” The basis he names is care for the hungry, thirsty, stranger, naked, sick, and imprisoned. They are astonished: when did we do these things? “As you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me.” The goats are told to depart into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels. Neither group is aware of the full significance of what they did. The sheep did not do these things to earn a reward; their love was the fruit of a transformed heart. The goats’ lack of love revealed that they did not know him.

Paul writes with sobering clarity: “For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ.” It says “all,” including Christians. And he draws the implication: “Therefore, knowing the fear of the Lord, we persuade others.” But he also explains the ground of confidence: “For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God” (2 Corinthians 5:21). We can look forward to the day not because we are good but because we are covered in Christ’s righteousness.
connection: Acts 17:30-31 and Romans 2:5-16 speak of the day of judgment. John 5:22-29 says the Father has given all judgment to the Son. 1 Corinthians 3:10-15 and 4:5 speak of the testing of works. Romans 14:10-12 says we will all stand before God’s judgment seat. Hebrews 9:27 says people die once and then face judgment. Ecclesiastes 12:14 says God will bring every deed into judgment. Daniel 12:1-3 speaks of resurrection to everlasting life and contempt. Romans 8:1 and John 5:24 promise no condemnation for believers. 2 Peter 3:7-9 speaks of the patience of God. Ezekiel 18:23 says God takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked.
application:
Take a few minutes to thank Christ for bearing the judgment you deserved. Read Romans 8:1 aloud.

Ask who in your life does not yet know Christ, and pray for them by name. Take one step to speak to them.

Look at Matthew 25 and ask: whom might you serve this week as if you were serving Christ himself?
prayerPrompts: Thank Jesus for being judge and also the one who bore judgment for you.
Tell him what you want to say about the final judgment.
Pray for someone you love who does not yet trust him.
